claims.text: A machine-learned interatomic potential trained on ab initio liquid snapshots will expand reference–target phase-space overlap.
The machine-learned reference will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to standard EAM references.
The target materials are multicomponent high-entropy alloys containing up to five principal elements in solid and near-liquid states at approximately 1400–2000 K.
The proposed intervention is to replace the EAM reference in TOR-TILD or a similar method with a machine-learned potential trained on liquid configurations of the same alloy.
The intervention is applicable to multi-principal-element systems such as CoCrFeMnNi within ±200 K of their melting point.
A liquid-trained machine-learned potential will more accurately represent variable coordination environments in disordered high-entropy liquids than an EAM reference.
A liquid-trained machine-learned potential will more accurately represent variable bonding environments in disordered high-entropy liquids than an EAM reference.
Training on liquid-like ab initio configurations reduces extrapolation during free-energy integration.
Reduced extrapolation lowers bias caused by atomic configurations missing from EAM reference sampling.
Transferable structural descriptors contribute to the expected improvement.
On-the-fly refinement during sampling contributes to the expected improvement.
The intervention is predicted to reduce the free-energy discrepancy between reference-based and fully ab initio calculations by approximately 25–40% or more.
The intervention will improve consistency between reference and ab initio ensemble-averaged liquid properties.
Existing TOR-TILD calculations using EAM references exhibit larger systematic errors in high-temperature or liquid free energies for many-component alloys.
The proposed approach is expected to remain effective across the solid–liquid range of high-entropy alloys.
Accuracy may deteriorate for strongly off-stoichiometric compositions or temperatures well below 1000 K when those conditions lie outside the training set.
The magnitude of improvement depends on whether the training set covers the important liquid microstates.
Residual errors may result from potential functional limitations or rare events absent from the training data.
The proposed benchmark compares machine-learned-reference, EAM-reference, and direct ab initio free energies near the melting point while also comparing sampled structural and dynamical observables.

The hypothesis is falsified if the machine-learned reference does not produce a statistically significant reduction in free-energy discrepancy relative to EAM in more than 50% of tested compositional variations.
